explanations.explanation: David inquires of the LORD first, and the question is simple: "Should I go and attack these Philistines?" He prays before he packs a single thing. Most of us text three friends and check the weather before we get around to that. And the LORD tells him, "Go and attack the Philistines and save Keilah."

No spies in this verse, friend. Nobody gets sent ahead to look around. The verse says David "inquired of the LORD," and that's where his first move goes. The answer he gets is, "Go and attack the Philistines and save Keilah."

The text doesn't have David calling in any brothers here. His men are with him, and they show up in the very next verse. David's first move is to inquire of the LORD. That's the move I'd want to copy, because my first move is usually to open the cookie jar and think.

Afraid is the word, and they say it plainly: "Look, we are afraid here in Judah." These men are already nervous with Saul hunting them, and now they're being asked to walk toward an army. I honestly respect them for saying it out loud. Then they ask, "how much more if we go to Keilah against the armies of the Philistines?"

Restless would mean they're itching to go, and that's the opposite of what they say. Their word is "afraid." They tell David, "Look, we are afraid here in Judah," and then they ask how much more afraid they'd be at Keilah. These men are not itching for anything.

Comfortable, with Saul out there hunting them? No ma'am, no sir. The men say, "Look, we are afraid here in Judah." They're nervous right where they stand, and they want to know what happens when they march toward the Philistine armies.

True. The verse says, "Once again, David inquired of the LORD." His men are scared, and David doesn't just pick a side. He takes the matter straight back to the LORD. I think that's a good habit when everybody around you is nervous and you'd like a steadier voice than your own.
The text says the opposite. After his men push back, "Once again, David inquired of the LORD." So he asks a second time, and he doesn't settle it by committee. Then the LORD answers him again.

The LORD promises, "I will deliver the Philistines into your hand." He says it right alongside "Go at once to Keilah." That's a promise David's frightened men can lean on. Marching toward an army is easier when the One sending you has already spoken about how it ends.

explanations.answer: He'll send a storm against them
explanations.explanation: No storm is mentioned here. The LORD's words are, "I will deliver the Philistines into your hand." Into David's hand, meaning David and his men go and fight. The fighting happens in the next verse.

The LORD doesn't say anything about scaring them away. His promise is, "I will deliver the Philistines into your hand." And that's what happens, because David and his men fight them at Keilah (1 Samuel 23:5). Nobody gets to skip the battle on this one.

They carried off the Philistines' livestock. The same Philistines who were looting Keilah's threshing floors end up losing their own animals. The text says David and his men struck them "with a mighty blow" too, so the livestock came with the win. It's a fair swap.

Weapons aren't mentioned at Keilah. The verse says David and his men "carried off their livestock." That's the only loot the text names. I'm sure there was plenty of other stuff lying around, but I only give you what the verse gives me.

The verse doesn't mention chariots. What it names is livestock: they "carried off their livestock." Chariots would be hard to sneak out anyway. Livestock walk on their own, which makes the hauling a lot easier.

Saul's reasoning is that David "has trapped himself by entering a town with gates and bars." To Saul, a walled town with a gate is a box with one way in. Gates that keep the Philistines out could also keep David in. Saul sees a trap, and he says God has delivered David into his hand.

The Philistines had been attacking Keilah, but David and his men struck them with a mighty blow (1 Samuel 23:5). Saul's reason is different. He says David "has trapped himself by entering a town with gates and bars." The gates are the whole point of his plan.

His men haven't gone anywhere. David leaves Keilah with about six hundred men (1 Samuel 23:13). Saul's reason is the town itself: David "has trapped himself by entering a town with gates and bars." He's counting on the gates, not on David being alone.
That one flips it. David asks, "Will Saul come down, as Your servant has heard?" and the LORD answers, "He will." So the report David heard is true. Saul is coming down to Keilah.

False is right, because the LORD says the opposite. David asks whether Saul will come down, and the answer is, "He will." What David heard about Saul's plan is true. That's exactly why David asks the next question about the people of Keilah.

True. David asks, "Will the citizens of Keilah surrender me and my men into the hand of Saul?" and the LORD says, "They will." It's a hard answer to hear, since David just saved those people. But he asked, he got a clear answer, and he knew what to do next.

The LORD actually says the opposite. David asks whether the citizens of Keilah will surrender him and his men into Saul's hand, and the answer is, "They will." David asked because he wanted to know before it was too late. And he left the town, so he never found out the hard way.

Saul had called up his troops, and then he hears David has escaped and he declines to go forth. The plan fell apart the moment David walked out of the gates. I think a man who was sure he had David trapped has a rough afternoon after that news. Saul doesn't march to Keilah.
The text never says Saul punishes Keilah. What it says is, "he declined to go forth." David had already left, and Saul stays put. Keilah is not mentioned again in the story.

Doeg, the Edomite who told Saul where David had gone (1 Samuel 22:9-10), isn't in this verse at all. Saul is told that David escaped, and then the text says he "declined to go forth." No one gets sent out.

The verse says it directly: "Day after day Saul searched for him, but God would not deliver David into his hand." Saul has the army and the free time, and it still doesn't work. I think that's the part to remember when everything looks like it's closing in. God is the One keeping David out of Saul's hands.

No fight happens in this verse. The reason it gives is, "God would not deliver David into his hand." David stays in the wilderness strongholds, and Saul keeps searching. The reason Saul doesn't get him is God, not a battle.

The text never says Saul's troops refuse anything. Saul searches "day after day," and the verse tells us why it doesn't work: "God would not deliver David into his hand." That's the only reason it gives.

It's Jonathan, Saul's son, who "came to David in Horesh and strengthened his hand in God." Saul is out hunting David, and his own son shows up to encourage him. Of all the people to walk up to David right then, that's the one nobody saw coming. I think David was glad to see him.

Abner, Saul's army commander (1 Samuel 14:50), isn't the visitor. The one who comes to David in Horesh is "Saul's son Jonathan." And he comes to strengthen David's hand in God, which is the opposite of an army coming to find him.
Samuel, the prophet, isn't in this scene. The text says "Saul's son Jonathan came to David in Horesh and strengthened his hand in God." The visitor is family to Saul, and he's there to help David.

explanations.answer: Saul will never lay a hand on him
explanations.explanation: Jonathan says, "Do not be afraid, for my father Saul will never lay a hand on you." He says it to a man who's being hunted at that very moment. That's a bold thing to tell somebody. And it comes from Saul's own son.

Jonathan never says Saul has forgiven David. The text has Saul out to take David's life (1 Samuel 23:15), so that would be a strange thing to say. What Jonathan says is, "my father Saul will never lay a hand on you."

explanations.answer: Saul will make him a commander
explanations.explanation: Jonathan doesn't say anything about Saul promoting David. Saul is out to take David's life. What Jonathan says is, "my father Saul will never lay a hand on you." The only second-in-command Jonathan mentions is himself, under David.

Jonathan says, "you will be king over Israel." That's a big thing to say to a man hiding in the wilderness with nothing but his men and some caves. Saul is still on the throne, and Jonathan is talking about what's coming. It's the kind of encouragement a hunted man can actually use.
Jonathan doesn't use the word judge. He says, "you will be king over Israel." King is a big word, and he says it right to David's face.
Priest isn't the word Jonathan uses. He tells David, "you will be king over Israel." He's talking about the throne, not the altar.

True. Jonathan says, "you will be king over Israel, and I will be your second-in-command." Think about that. The king's own son, the one next in line, says he'll happily stand beneath David. That's a rare kind of friend.

The text says the opposite. Jonathan tells David, "you will be king over Israel, and I will be your second-in-command." Jonathan is the king's son, and he's picking the second spot under David. He means it, too.
True. Jonathan says, "Even my father Saul knows this is true." So Saul knows David will be king. That helps explain why a man with an army is spending his days chasing one man through the wilderness.
The text says otherwise. Jonathan tells David, "Even my father Saul knows this is true." The "this" is that David will be king over Israel. Saul knows it, and he's still out searching for David.

They "made a covenant before the LORD." A covenant is a serious promise between two people, made in front of God. After that, David stays in Horesh and Jonathan goes home. It's a quiet goodbye, and it's a promise they'll keep.
No sacrifice is mentioned here. The verse says the two of them "made a covenant before the LORD." That's a solemn promise, and the text doesn't say they did anything more than that.
The text mentions no pillar. What David and Jonathan do is "make a covenant before the LORD." It's a promise made between two friends, with God watching. Then Jonathan goes home.

The Ziphites ask Saul, "Is not David hiding among us in the strongholds at Horesh?" They give his hiding place straight to Saul. They even say where it is: the hill of Hachilah, south of Jeshimon. Hiding is the whole situation David is in.

Fighting isn't the word they use. They tell Saul, "Is not David hiding among us in the strongholds at Horesh?" David isn't out there fighting anyone at that moment. He's hiding, and the Ziphites are the ones who point him out.
Ruling isn't what the Ziphites say. They say, "Is not David hiding among us in the strongholds at Horesh?" Jonathan has just told David he will be king, but right now David is hiding, not ruling.

Saul tells them, "Observe and find out all the places where he hides. Then come back to me with certainty." He's been told David is extremely cunning, so he wants the full picture first. Only then does he say, "I will go with you." He's asking them to scout, and he'll do the rest.

The Ziphites offered to be responsible for delivering David (1 Samuel 23:20), but Saul says something different. He asks them to find out all the places David hides and come back, and then he says, "I will go with you." He's not sending them out to do the capturing alone.
Saul never asks them to lure anyone. His words are, "Observe and find out all the places where he hides." He wants information first. Then he says he'll go with them.

The text says otherwise. When David is told Saul is coming, "he went down to the rock and stayed in the Wilderness of Maon." He doesn't leave the wilderness. He goes down to the rock, and he stays there.
False is right. When David hears about Saul's search, he "went down to the rock and stayed in the Wilderness of Maon." So he stays in the same wilderness. Saul hears about it and pursues him there.

explanations.answer: A messenger brings news of a raid
explanations.explanation: Right when Saul is closing in, a messenger comes and says, "Come quickly, for the Philistines have raided the land!" Saul is on one side of the mountain, David is on the other, and then everything changes. It's the kind of interruption you would never plan for. And Saul breaks off the chase.

explanations.answer: David's men turn and fight back
explanations.explanation: No one turns and fights back here. David is hurrying to get away. What stops the chase is a messenger who says, "Come quickly, for the Philistines have raided the land!"

explanations.answer: A storm stops Saul's whole army
explanations.explanation: The text mentions no storm. What interrupts Saul is a messenger, who says, "Come quickly, for the Philistines have raided the land!" It's news that pulls Saul away, not weather.

True. The messenger says the Philistines have raided the land, and "Saul broke off his pursuit of David and went to meet the Philistines." The chase just stops. That's why that place is called Sela-hammahlekoth. And David goes up from there.

The text says it plainly: "Saul broke off his pursuit of David and went to meet the Philistines." So Saul does stop chasing David after the messenger's news. The place gets its name Sela-hammahlekoth because of it. David then goes up to the strongholds of En-gedi.
